# Blocked Input Tax Credit (CGST Act, Section 17(5))

Input Tax Credit is NOT available (it is "blocked") on certain inward supplies even
if used for business, except where specifically allowed. Key blocked items:

- Motor vehicles for transport of persons with seating capacity up to 13 (including
 driver), except when used for further supply of such vehicles, passenger
 transport, or driving training.
- Food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, cosmetic
 and plastic surgery — except where used to make an outward taxable supply of the
 same category or where it is obligatory for an employer to provide to employees
 under any law.
- Membership of a club, health and fitness centre.
- Rent-a-cab, life insurance and health insurance — except where obligatory under law.
- Travel benefits to employees on vacation (leave or home travel concession).

# Input Tax Credit — eligibility and conditions (CGST Act, Section 16)

A registered person is entitled to take credit of input tax charged on inward
supplies of goods or services used or intended to be used in the course or
furtherance of business, subject to conditions. The credit is credited to the
electronic credit ledger.

Conditions to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC):
- The registered person must possess a tax invoice or debit note issued by a
 registered supplier.
- The details of the invoice must have been furnished by the supplier and must
 appear in the recipient's auto-drafted statement (GSTR-2B) — credit is restricted
 to invoices so communicated.
- The recipient must have received the goods or services.
- The tax charged must have actually been paid to the Government by the supplier.
- The recipient must have furnished the return under Section 39 (e.g. GSTR-3B).

# GST registration — threshold and liability (CGST Act, Section 22; with CBIC threshold notifications)

Every supplier is liable to be registered under GST in the State/UT from where they
make a taxable supply of goods or services once their aggregate turnover in a
financial year exceeds the prescribed threshold.

Threshold limits for compulsory registration (aggregate turnover, all-India PAN basis):
- Suppliers of GOODS (normal category States): more than Rs. 40 lakh.
- Suppliers of SERVICES (normal category States): more than Rs. 20 lakh.
- Special category States (and some others): more than Rs. 20 lakh for goods and
 more than Rs. 10 lakh for services.

"Aggregate turnover" includes taxable, exempt, export and inter-State supplies of a
person on the same PAN, computed all-India, but excludes GST itself.

# Deduction under Section 80C (Income-tax Act, 1961)

Section 80C allows an individual or HUF a deduction from gross total income for
specified investments and payments, up to an aggregate ceiling of Rs. 1,50,000 in a
financial year (the combined 80C + 80CCC + 80CCD(1) limit).

Common eligible items include:
- Employee Provident Fund (EPF) and Public Provident Fund (PPF) contributions.
- Life insurance premium (within prescribed limits relative to sum assured).
- Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) units.
- Principal repayment of a housing loan; stamp duty and registration on a house.
- 5-year tax-saving bank fixed deposit; National Savings Certificate (NSC).
- Sukanya Samriddhi Account; tuition fees for up to two children.

Important: deductions under Chapter VI-A such as 80C are available under the OLD tax
regime. They are generally NOT available under the default NEW regime

# Income-tax return — due dates and late fee (Income-tax Act, Section 139, 234F)

Due date for filing the Income-tax Return (ITR) under Section 139(1) for a normal
financial year, unless extended by the Department:
- 31 July of the assessment year — individuals/HUF and others whose accounts are NOT
 required to be audited.
- 31 October of the assessment year — taxpayers whose accounts are required to be
 audited (e.g. companies, and others subject to tax audit).
- 30 November of the assessment year — taxpayers required to furnish a transfer-
 pricing report (Section 92E).

A belated return can be filed under Section 139(4), and a revised return under
Section 139(5), up to 31 December of the assessment year (or before completion of
assessment, whichever is earlier). An updated return (ITR-U) under Section 139(8A)
has its own extended window.

# Presumptive taxation for small business and professionals (Income-tax Act, Sections 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE)

Section 44AD — eligible resident business (not profession), individual / HUF /
partnership firm (not LLP), with turnover up to the prescribed limit:
- Profit is presumed at 8% of turnover/gross receipts.
- The presumed rate is 6% for the part of turnover received through banking channels
 (account-payee cheque/draft, ECS, or other prescribed electronic modes).
- Turnover ceiling is Rs. 2 crore; it is raised to Rs. 3 crore where cash receipts
 do not exceed 5% of total turnover.
- If a person opts out of 44AD after opting in, they are barred from claiming it for
 the next five assessment years.

Section 44ADA — eligible resident professionals (e.g. legal, medical, engineering,
architecture, accountancy, technical consultancy, interior decoration):

Section 44AE — presumptive scheme for the business of plying, hiring or leasing
